sports-injuries.p2: From there, we build a progressive plan that restores tissue capacity, re-educates movement patterns, and prepares you for a safe return to your sport.

faq.title: Answers before we begin
faq.description: The questions I hear most often from patients considering this service.

q1.question: How many sessions will I need?
q1.answer: It depends on the injury and your goals. Most patients see meaningful progress within 4–6 sessions, with a full return to sport often taking 8–12 weeks. We'll set clear milestones from the first session.

q2.question: Do I need a doctor's referral?
q2.answer: No referral is required to book a session. If imaging or specialist input is needed, I'll guide you on the next steps.

q3.question: Can I keep training while recovering?
q3.answer: In most cases, yes — with modifications. We'll identify what you can safely continue and build the rest of the plan around it.

q4.question: When can I return to competition?
q4.answer: Return to competition is based on objective readiness tests (strength, balance, sport-specific movement). We won't clear you until every criterion is met — even if pain is gone.

q1.question: Is my back pain caused by a disc herniation?
q1.answer: In many cases, pain isn't driven by a single cause. Assessment will clarify whether there's a specific structural issue or whether pain is related to load and movement patterns we can change.

q2.question: Is bed rest helpful?
q2.answer: Prolonged rest often makes back pain worse. Guided movement and progressive loading are the most powerful tools for restoring spine function.

q3.question: Will I need imaging (X-ray or MRI)?
q3.answer: Usually not, unless warning signs appear during assessment. Most back pain cases are managed successfully without imaging.

q4.question: Will I keep exercising after recovery?
q4.answer: Yes. The goal is for you to own a clear routine you can maintain long-term — without needing ongoing sessions.

q1.question: Should I stop moving to reduce pain?
q1.answer: No. Guided movement is the foundation of recovery. We'll modify activity rather than stop it, so you preserve range of motion and muscle strength.

q2.question: Does joint pain mean irreversible wear?
q2.answer: Not necessarily. Many joint pain cases improve significantly with rehabilitation, even when imaging shows mild wear.

q3.question: Will pain increase with exercise?
q3.answer: Mild temporary discomfort during loading is normal. We'll calibrate intensity so pain stays tolerable and doesn't worsen after the session.

q4.question: How long until I see improvement?
q4.answer: Most patients notice better movement and less pain within 3–4 weeks. Full improvement depends on the joint and how consistently you follow the program.

q1.question: When should rehab start after surgery?
q1.answer: Rehab usually starts within days of surgery — even gently. The earlier it begins with proper supervision, the better the outcome.

q2.question: Will I return to my previous level?
q2.answer: The goal is always to return at or above your previous level. The result depends on the surgery, your consistency, and the quality of the rehab program.

q3.question: How long does rehabilitation take?
q3.answer: It varies. Some patients return to daily activities within 4–6 weeks, while a full return to sport can take 3 to 6 months.

q4.question: Do I need multiple sessions per week?
q4.answer: Early stages may require two sessions per week. After that, we reduce frequency and rely more on your home program.

q1.question: What's the difference between sports rehab and general rehab?
q1.answer: Sports rehab is designed to prepare you for the specific demands of your sport — with strength, coordination, and readiness testing. General rehab focuses on daily activities.

q2.question: Will I train using movements from my sport?
q2.answer: Yes, at the right stage. We start with general work, then progress to sport-specific movements under load before full return.

q3.question: How do you know I'm ready to return?
q3.answer: We use objective tests: muscle strength, jump capacity, balance, and sport-specific movement. Return only happens when every criterion is passed.

q4.question: How do I prevent re-injury?
q4.answer: By building lasting strength and balance, and continuing a preventive routine after return. I'll give you a short program you can stick with long-term.
